title: Three highest-priority Topic 6.5 Bernoulli scenario model assumptions for teacher decision
sourceOriginalPrintedQuestionProvenance: Teacher-prepared master PDF pp.190–193; printed original NBF pp.99–100 confirms the Bernoulli relation, not the verbatim proposed questions
releaseConstraints: No student bank, PDF export, SLO ledger, Test Builder availability, Firebase security or academic release edits. Approved wording must be separately authorized before an implementation PR.

candidates.originalStem: A smooth horizontal pipe narrows from section X to section Y, and water flows steadily. Relative to X, Y has:

originalOptions.text: Lower speed and higher static pressure
Higher speed and higher static pressure
Unchanged speed and unchanged static pressure
Higher speed and lower static pressure

candidates.proposedStem: In a horizontal, unbranched pipe, water flows steadily and incompressibly from a wider section X to a narrower section Y. Assume negligible viscous losses, no pumps or turbines, and compare points on the same streamline. Relative to X, Y has:

proposedOptions.text: Lower speed and higher static pressure
Higher speed and higher static pressure
Unchanged speed and unchanged static pressure
Higher speed and lower static pressure

candidates.independentExplanation: Conservation of volume discharge gives AX vX = AY vY. Because AY is smaller, vY is larger. Along the same horizontal ideal streamline without head loss or shaft work, PX + (ρvX²)/2 = PY + (ρvY²)/2, so PY - PX = (ρ/2)(vX² - vY²) < 0. Thus section Y has higher speed and lower static pressure (D).
workedPhysics: Incompressible steady leak-free continuity: AX vX = AY vY.
Ideal same-height Bernoulli: PY − PX = (ρ/2)(vX² − vY²) < 0.
Therefore original answer D remains correct, conditionally.
candidates.whyClarify: Smooth pipe and steady water flow do not alone establish the ideal Bernoulli pressure outcome. A decrease in area yields higher speed by steady incompressible continuity; static pressure is lower only in the stated no-loss/no-shaft-work same-elevation same-streamline model.
limitations: Viscous pipe losses and pump/turbine energy invalidate the simple no-loss pressure inference.
Formative SLO P-11-B-39 must not be silently mapped as summative theory; P-11-B-40 item-level mapping remains pending.

candidates.originalStem: A water stream rises in a tube of unchanged area. Which pair of energy terms is unchanged and increased, respectively?

originalOptions.text: Pressure term increased; gravitational term decreased
Kinetic term decreased; gravitational term decreased
Kinetic term unchanged; gravitational term increased
Kinetic term increased; gravitational term unchanged

candidates.proposedStem: Water flows steadily and incompressibly without leaks through an unbranched tube of constant cross-sectional area, rising from a lower section to a higher one. Which pair of energy terms is unchanged and increased, respectively?

proposedOptions.text: Pressure term increased; gravitational term decreased
Kinetic term decreased; gravitational term decreased
Kinetic term unchanged; gravitational term increased
Kinetic term increased; gravitational term unchanged

candidates.independentExplanation: For an unbranched, leak-free, steady incompressible stream, the discharge Q = Av is constant. Since A is the same at both stations, v is the same, so ½ρv² is unchanged. The higher point has greater ρgh, so the gravitational energy term increases. The source correct answer remains C. This alone does not guarantee individual FBISE B40 Application certification.
workedPhysics: Steady incompressible continuity: Q = A1v1 = A2v2.
A1 = A2 and no leaks/branches imply v1 = v2.
The kinetic energy-density term ½ρv² remains unchanged.
For h2 > h1, the gravitational energy-density term ρgh increases; original answer C.
candidates.whyClarify: Equal area alone does not guarantee equal velocities in time-varying or compressible flow or if fluid leaks or branches. Clarify constant discharge, no leaks and density, then the original kinetic and gravitational energy claims follow.
limitations: Unsteady flow and compressible density variation may defeat a universal inference from equal area.
This uses continuity in support of Bernoulli, so P-11-B-36 vs P-11-B-40 and item cognition require separate review.

candidates.originalStem: A fluid moves steadily in a horizontal pipe with the same cross-sectional area at both points. Ignoring losses and pumps, its static pressures are:
candidates.proposedStem: An incompressible fluid flows steadily through an unbranched horizontal pipe of equal cross-sectional area at points X and Y. Assume both points lie on the same streamline, with negligible viscous losses and no pumps or turbines between them. The static pressures at X and Y are:
candidates.independentExplanation: For steady incompressible no-leak flow, Q = Av is constant. Equal AX and AY give vX = vY. Because both points are horizontal and the same ideal lossless streamline is used, PX + ½ρvX² = PY + ½ρvY²; hence PX = PY (C). Compressible flow can have different densities and speeds at equal area, so the original unqualified premise was under-specified.
workedPhysics: Steady incompressible continuity: AX vX = AY vY.
At equal height, ideal Bernoulli implies PX + ½ρvX² = PY + ½ρvY².
Therefore PX = PY under the stated model, original answer C.
candidates.whyClarify: The original says a fluid with equal areas, which does not enforce constant density. Steady compressible mass continuity ρAv = constant permits different speeds at the same area; static pressure need not be equal. State incompressibility and ideal Bernoulli conditions.
limitations: For compressible flow, constant mass rate ρAv—not equal area alone—governs speed, and pressures may differ.
Real flow pressure losses also make equal static pressure invalid unless negligible as explicitly stated.
